That's the point and I don't say anything further, but that's the point of our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will MFI the document. Mr. Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D936, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D936 is marked for identification and the Chamber will, in due course, decide on the admission as requested by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and that would be -- have you uploaded the relevant pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I haven't. Still need to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still needs to be done, so D936 is reserved for the extract of the court proceedings in the case against Mr. Mandic, both covering the testimony of Mr. Delimustafic and some other portions as well. In accordance with the pages mentioned by Mr. Ivetic, and once it's uploaded, we'd like to hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You will, Your Honours. We're at the time for the break. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to thank you Mr. Karisik on behalf of the Defence team for coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And thank you, Your Honours for the extra time that we went over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we take that break, could I inquire with the Prosecution if you have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one further question. Please answer briefly. We see your statement from the Karadzic case and quite a number of paragraphs have been redacted, removed, more or less, blackened out. Could you tell us how this happened? Did you suggest to take those portions out, or did it happen in any other way? Could you just briefly describe how this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A certain number of generals thought that this should be my statement that should be based on my previous statement --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the first part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first part was not well captured by our interpreters. Could you please repeat what you said in the beginning of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence team of General Mladic, that was the first part. They redacted my statement because they thought that to be necessary for this case, for this trial, and this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. May I take it that my question has not triggered any further --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I could tell that you in keeping with your guidance we redacted the statements. The unredacted is available in e-court as 1D4749 without the A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll not look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we take that the Prosecution has done so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karisik, this concludes your evidence. I'd like to thank you very much for coming the long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you - sometimes even more than that - questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. You may follow the usher. I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break, and we'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we invite the Defence to call its next witness, there are a few procedural items I'd like to briefly deal with. The first one is the Defence has asked for additional time to prepare for the reopening of the Prosecution's case. When could the Chamber expect the response by the Prosecution? Because we considered it be an urgent matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Mr. President. I think certainly in the next two days. It shouldn't take us long. We do need to just focus on it, and speak to our superiors. But that shouldn't be a problem. I would hope within two days. We'll let you know if there's any delay in that. Normally, as you know, as Mr. Tieger said, this is the kind of thing we leave in your hands, but we need to take a closer look at this, see if we could be of help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the Chamber would very much appreciate that you respond as quickly as possible so that we can further consider the matter. And, of course, it has an impact on all kinds of plans and scheduling issues and therefore we'd like to deal with it as quickly as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to deal with a few matters and read two decisions. First one deals with the admission of P7049. On the 21st and the 22nd of January of this year, the Prosecution and the Defence used excerpts of document bearing 65 ter number 14008 with Prosecution -- with the Witness -- not a Prosecution witness, GRM014. Exhibit number P7049 was reserved for the document pending agreement between the parties as to which pages would be tendered. You can find this on transcript page 30439 through 30440. On 22 January the Prosecution informed the Chamber that it had uploaded an excerpt into e-court under 65 ter number 14008a and requested that it be admitted. The Chamber is inviting the Defence to express itself on whether it has any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will inform you about that tomorrow morning because my colleague, Mr. Lukic, is dealing with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait for your answer and receive it tomorrow morning. Then there is a remaining issue from the testimony of Slavko Puhalic, it's about D899. During the testimony of this witness on 12 February 2015, D899, a video, was marked for identification pending information from the Defence on the date, location where it was filmed, and a number of sequences in the video. This can be found at transcript pages 31649 to 31651. On the 9th of February, the Defence informed the Chamber that D899 was taped on the 5th of August, 1992 and is an excerpt of 65 ter number 22615, which also is a video. This can be found at transcript pages 32740 to -741. The Chamber notes that the Defence did not provide any information on where the video had been filmed or on the number of sequences included in the video, as requested by the Chamber on the 4th of March at transcript page 32636. The Chamber therefore denies the admission of D899 into evidence without prejudice. Then I'll deliver the oral decision on the expertise of Bruno Franjic related to the Tomasica mass grave. On the 26th of August, 2014, the Prosecution filed a notice of disclosure of Bruno Franjic's expert report related to the Tomasica mass grave, pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. On the 18th of September, the Chamber granted the Defence request of the 8th of September for an extension of time to file its Rule 94 bis (B) notice. The Defence responded on the 22nd of December, objecting to the Prosecution's notice of disclosure of expert reports related to the Tomasica mass grave. The Defence submits that the Prosecution be ordered to supplement its submission regarding Franjic to meet the minimum threshold required by Rule 94 bis or, in the alternative, that Franjic be disqualified as an expert and that his report be rejected. It submits that the conclusions in the report tend to fall outside the scope of his expertise and that there's a suspicion of bias that impacts on the impartiality of the report. With respect to the applicable law concerning expert evidence, the Chamber recalls and refers to its 19th of October 2012 decision concerning Richard Butler. On the basis of Franjic's curriculum vitae, the Chamber is satisfied that he has specialised knowledge in the field of ballistic analysis. Such knowledge may be of assistance to the Chamber in understanding issues related to the evidence on the exhumation of the Tomasica grave-site. With regard to the Defence request to cross-examine the witness, the Chamber notes that the Prosecution plans to call Franjic as part of its reopening case. The Defence will therefore have the opportunity to cross-examine him. As for any of the arguments raised by the Defence related to the reliability and exceeding of expertise of Franjic's report, the Chamber considers that these are matters that can be, and should be, addressed during the cross-examination of the witness. The Defence will also have an opportunity to fully explore the witness's alleged bias in the course of cross-examination or can address it by means of an expert opinion in reply. Based on the foregoing, the Chamber decides, pursuant to Rule 94 bis, that Witness Franjic may be called to testify as an expert witness and shall be made available for cross-examination by the Defence; denies the Defence request to order the Prosecution to supplement its submission; and denies the Defence request to disqualify Franjic as an expert. The Chamber defers its decision on admission of the report and its addendum to the time of the witness's testimony. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. I will now deliver a decision of a similar nature. A decision on the expertise of Elmira Karahasanovic, in regard to the exhumation of the Tomasica mass grave. On the 26th of August 2014, the Prosecution filed a notice of disclosure of Elmira Karahasanovic's expert report related to the Tomasica mass grave pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. On 18th September, the Chamber granted the Defence request of the 8th of September for an extension of time to file its Rule 94 bis (B) notice. The Defence responded on 22nd of December, objecting to the Prosecution's notice of disclosure of expert reports related to the Tomasica mass grave. The Defence submits that the Prosecution be ordered to supplement its submission regarding Witness Karahasanovic to meet the minimum threshold required by Rule 94 bis or, alternatively, that Karahasanovic be disqualified as an expert than her report be rejected. The Defence contends that the report exceeds the scope of her expertise. The Defence further challenges the methodology and reliability of the proffered report. With respect to the applicable law concerning expert evidence, the Chamber recalls and refers to its decision of the 19th of October, 2012, concerning Richard Butler. On the basis of Karahasanovic's curriculum vitae, the Chamber is satisfied that she has specialised knowledge in the field of forensic pathology. Such knowledge may be of assistance to the Chamber in understanding issues related to the evidence on the exhumation of the Tomasica grave-site. With regard to the Defence request to cross-examine the witness, the Chamber notes that the Prosecution plans to call Karahasanovic as part of its reopening case. The Defence will therefore have the opportunity to cross-examine her. As for any of the arguments raised by the Defence related to the methodology, reliability, and exceeding of expertise of Karahasanovic's report, the Chamber considers that these are matters that can be, and should be, addressed during the cross-examination of the witness. Based on the foregoing, the Chamber decides, pursuant to Rule 94 bis, that Witness Karahasanovic may be called to testify as an expert witness and shall be made available for cross-examination by the Defence; denies the Defence request to order the Prosecution to supplement its submission; and denies the Defence request to disqualify Elmira Karahasanovic as an expert. The Chamber defers its decision on admission of the report and photodocumentation to the time of the witness's testimony. And this concludes the Chamber's decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Dragoslav Trisic is a reserve officer. In April 1992 he was mobilised by the Ministry of Defence in Bratunac. He was assigned to discharge the duties as a Chief of Staff of the TO. At that time, the TO commander was Captain Momir Nikolic. When the VRS was established, he discharged a series of duties and finally he was appointed the assistant commander of the Bratunac Brigade for logistics. He remained in that position until the end of the war. In his statement, he speaks about his activities which preceded the events known as Krivaja 95 and the tasks that he had at the time. He provides a detailed description of the tasks of his service pursuant to the preparatory order of the Drina Corps dated 2nd July 1992. He also describes the tasks that were issued to his brigade based on the order for active combat in Operation Krivaja 95. He also mentions his handwritten suggestions to his commander and also suggestions by Momir Nikolic based on his opinion. Finally, he explains the tasks based on the order of the commander of the Bratunac Brigade dated 5 July 1992, which were based on the order of the Drina Corps Command. He received the information on the liberation of Srebrenica on the 11th of July, 1995. Already on the 12th of July 1992 or, rather, 1995 he remembers that a telegram was received from the assistant commander of the Drina Corps for logistics. According to that telegram, vehicles had to be deployed to transport Muslims, those Muslims who had gathered in Potocari and also that the population should be provided with all the available quantities of bread. When he embarked on the implementation of the order, he went to Potocari where he saw General Mladic. General Mladic addressed the people there and told them that they would be transported to Tuzla and that there was no need for them to create havoc, and that was received by the people with approval. He stayed there for an hour to an hour and a half and he did not see that men were separated from the group, nor that they were forbidden from entering the buses. He did not see any force being used against the population, nor did he hear any derogatory word used to refer to those people. That same afternoon, the 12th of July, 1995, he was at the command of the Bratunac Brigade, as well as on the following day, the 3rd [as interpreted] of July 1995. He heard that there had been shooting at the Kravica farm, that a Muslim had attacked a policeman, stole his rifle and killed him. The rest of the police who were providing security responded by opening fire in order to prevent people from fleeing. And, finally, he says that on 14th and 15th July, the Bratunac Brigade was involved in the scouring of the terrain. One part of the unit joined the Zvornik Brigade in its area of responsibility due to the problems with the column of the 28th Division of the BiH army, and on the 17th of July, one part of his brigade was deployed in the direction of Zepa. Your Honour, this was a short summary of Witness Dragoslav Trisic's statement, and now I would like to have a few questions for the witness. I would like to call up D937, paragraph 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trisic, I would like to ask you, in view of your duties, the duties that you discharged as the assistant commander for logistics in the Bratunac Brigade, in addition to the fuel that you received at the parking lot of the Vihor company, did you receive any other equipment, materiel, or supplies that were necessary for the implementation of your tasks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC
utterances.text: We received fuel from other sides as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, could you please tell us who you received the fuel from at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, in the afternoon, an UNPROFOR truck arrived in -- in the perimeter of the Vihor transport company. Within that perimeter there was a fuel tank which was used by the transport company itself. That truck that had arrived in the Vihor perimeter unloaded some 30 tonnes of diesel fuel for buses. Those buses were supposed to transport the Muslim population in the direction of either Tuzla or Kladanj. We received 30 tonnes of diesel fuel from UNPROFOR. Those UNPROFOR units were in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive additional quantities of fuel from other international organisations on top of the 30 tonnes that you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the following day, since a lot of fuel was being used for the buses, from UNHCR we received an additional 23.300 litres or 23,3 tonnes of diesel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could we please take a look at paragraph 26 of your statement now.

In principle, I was in that area of Zepa from the beginning until the end, until the brigade returned to the area of Bratunac.

utterances.text: I'm going to end by putting the following question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You tendered it as associated exhibit so I don't know that you need further -- I mean, the correspond is what everyone is read, is there anything else that needs to be clarified? Because what we have now, we have two pages in English, both more or less the same, I would say, and we have in the original, we have page 1 in e-court is the -- is the typewritten, better legible version. Page 2 contains only two numbers. Page 3, 4, and 5 is the handwriting the witness referred to earlier. Any further need to put further questions, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there are none, Your Honour. After the witness confirmed this, so now I would like to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The number had been reserved already. That was D938. D938 is admitted into evidence. Ms. Edgerton --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And I have thereby finished with the witness. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, would it not be better that we take a break now and that you then have 20 minutes left to start your cross-examination after the break. Or if Mr. Mladic would prefer to go on for another 20 minutes and then adjourn for the day, that would be agreeable to the Chamber as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you please switch on your microphone that we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just convey General Mladic's position and that is he thinks it's better that we take a break now and that we work for 20 minutes after that break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That suggestion is followed. The witness may now follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, and we'll resume at five minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trisic, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Edgerton. You'll find her to your right. Ms. Edgerton is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Trisic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm going to try and keep this as brief as I can, but, unfortunately, it might stretch out into a little bit of time tomorrow. So let's begin. Can you just confirm, first of all, that you stayed on duty in your post in the Bratunac Brigade long after the end of the war. You left in June 1996; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Great. Now, I'd just like to amplify some of the evidence you gave in your statement in paragraph 7 about how the brigade was supplied. So my first question is: You can confirm, can't you, that the VRS Main Staff had its own logistics centres; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they had their own logistics centres, the Main Staff did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how it worked is that when your units needed ammunition, fuel, whatever, they would ask the brigade, and then, depending on what was required, the brigade would ask the corps, and the corps would ask the Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The brigade would address the corps command with a request for replenishment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And during the operation you talked about in your written evidence, Krivaja 95, that's what happened, right, the Bratunac Brigade received large quantities of ammunition and materiel through this process; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now it's relative whether these were large quantities or not. At any rate, we did not get as much as we had asked for. We always got less. Because there wasn't enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And so -- and it came through you; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to have a quick look at one document so we can get some insight into how this process worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 06029.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So in front of you on the screen is a document from Milenko Lazic, who was the operations chief and Deputy Chief of Staff at the Drina Corps, and it's to the VRS Main Staff. And it's dated the 8th of July, 1995. So what he's doing is telling them that considering in the course of the day the brigade has conducted heavy offensive operations in Srebrenica territory, and met with some success, they consumed a large amount of ammunition of all calibres and they needed to replenish their supplies. So he asks for 7.62-millimetre bullets, I think the English translation is rounds but it's bullets, for different weapons. And have a look at the rest of the list so these 20-millimetre and 30-millimetre rounds, that's ammunition for anti-aircraft guns; right? Do you see the mention of 20 and 30-millimetre "metak," in your own language. It's at the bottom of the paragraph of this single document. That refers to ammunition for -- that's anti-aircraft ammunition; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is ammunition for two different guns. 20 millimetres and 30 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And these 90-millimetre rounds, that's ammunition for tanks; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it mentions 122-millimetre D-30 shells. Those are Howitzer rounds that they're talking about in this document, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC
utterances.text: I think so, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you got what you asked for, didn't you? Your brigade received these weapons, or pardon me, this ammunition as a result of this request. That's what happened; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Your Honours, I think that this leads to confusion because the question has to do with whether the Bratunac Brigade received this and this document is the command of the Drina Corps, so I don't think that the foundation has been laid properly for this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there has been laid a foundation as to the system; that is, brigade, corps, Main Staff. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So did you get these -- did you get the ammunition set out in this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC
utterances.text: No. This is not a request of the brigade. This is a request of the higher command, of the corps command, and it's addressed to the Main Staff of the VRS. So the request has nothing do with the brigade command or my authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's move that off the screen for a moment and go to 65 ter number 6306 which also dated from the 8th of July, 1995. Same date as this document. Right. Now, Mr. Trisic, this is a delivery note dated 8th of July, 1995 from military post 7111, Han Pijesak, and that's the Drina Corps Command to your military post. And, Mr. Trisic, it shows that on that date, the Bratunac Brigade received 7.62-millimetre bullets to the tune of 15.000; 7.9-millimetre bullets, 30-millimetre bullets, and it received 122-millimetre D-30 artillery shells.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is what the document says. I cannot say otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when you unequivocally denied receiving any of the ammunition that was outlined in the Lazic document from the Drina Corps, that was incorrect, wasn't it? That's confirmed by this document.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC
utterances.text: I still maintain that the command of the Bratunac Brigade or I, as assistant commander for logistics, did not ask for materiel or, rather, ammunition, as is stated in the request and as is stated in this material list. An explanation for that could be as follows: During the operation in Bratunac, logistics functioned of the command of the Drina Corps, that is, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we'll have a chance to hear an explanation, perhaps, in your re-direct examination. But let's go back to your response in respect of the first document that Mr. Lazic wrote. I asked you whether or not your brigade received any of the weaponry -- pardon me, the ammunition that was listed in that document, and you said no. 65 ter 6306 confirms your brigade received it, so I didn't ask you, with respect, whether or not you have actually requested the ammunition we're talking about. The fact is your brigade received it; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC
utterances.text: Our Bratunac Brigade did not need this ammunition, 30-millimetre, 100-millimetre bullets, because we did not have these artillery pieces. According to the document, somebody used this in order to have that ammunition delivered in the area of Bratunac. And that is why this is stated, but I maintain that we had not asked for this ammunition or, rather, we did not have artillery pieces for using this kind of ammunition, 30 millimetres, 100 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, could you answer my question. Did you receive it or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC
utterances.text: Well, according to the document that is stated that it arrived in the Bratunac Brigade. However, right now, I cannot remember. It was a long time ago. Now, whether it specifically arrived in our storage facilities or those of some other unit and the document says the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask for a clarification on this point. Sir, I see on the original a signature that looks like yours and on the English version, they said personally received by Major Trisic. Would that not be your signature and are you not the Major Trisic who received this equipment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we zoom in on the B/C/S, the lower right corner?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And even further. Still further. Yes, there we are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need. I can see everything and I accept that this is my signature. I signed this document. However, I don't remember. It was a long time ago. I don't remember how this document arrived and when. But it was not necessary for the Bratunac Brigade. That kind of ammunition was not needed for the Bratunac Brigade. This is all I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I then ask another question. Did you receive this kind -- ammunition on behalf of other units other than the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably on behalf of another unit of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But I see here the name and place of receipt is VP 7042 Bratunac. What does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we zoom out on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a military post, the military post of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So that's the brigade of which you were logistics assistant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, before we break could I just have these two documents 06209 [sic] and 6306 admitted as Prosecution Exhibits, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number to be assigned would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 06029 would be Exhibit P7221. And 06306 will be Exhibit P7222.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you could just have a look at the transcript and see because there's slight -- the first one, is that 06209 or 06029?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7221 and P7222 are admitted into evidence. Mr. Trisic, we'll adjourn for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30. But before you leave this courtroom, I instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, that is, testimony given today, or testimony still to be given tomorrow. If that is clear to you, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 18th of March, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
